review-neurips-2026-148395.title: Monitoring Violations of Differential Privacy over Time

checks.claim: \displaystyle\limsup_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\big(O=\textnormal{"DP violation detected"}\big)\leq\alpha.
checks.explanation: The studentized binomial score has a positive mean of order $n^{-1/2}$ at an admissible DP boundary. Over $T=n^2$ independent monitoring times, its full-window sum divided by $\sqrt T$ has a mean that diverges. The false-alarm probability therefore tends to one.
checks.demonstration:
Consider a binary mechanism, fixed over time, on two neighboring databases. On the first database its probability of output one is $p=3/5$; on the second it is $q=1/5$. Take $\varepsilon=\log3$. The probability ratio for output one is $3$, and the reverse ratio for output zero is $(1-q)/(1-p)=2$; their reciprocal ratios are also at most $3$. Thus the mechanism satisfies DP in both directions, and its gap $p-e^\varepsilon q$ is zero. Using the same mechanism at every time is permitted with $K=0$.

At each time, draw fresh independent samples of size $n$ from each output law. Write their proportions as $\hat p,\hat q$ and let
$$\hat v=\hat p(1-\hat p)+9\hat q(1-\hat q),\qquad Z_n=\frac{\sqrt n(\hat p-3\hat q)}{\sqrt{\hat v}}.$$
The corresponding population variance and third-moment coefficient are
$$v=p(1-p)+9q(1-q)=1.68,$$
$$\kappa=p(1-p)(1-2p)-27q(1-q)(1-2q)=-2.64.$$
Although the numerator is centered, it is correlated with its estimated denominator. Expanding the reciprocal square root around $v$ gives the bias term
$$\mathbb E Z_n=-\frac{\kappa}{2v^{3/2}\sqrt n}+O(n^{-3/2})=\frac{0.606191732\ldots}{\sqrt n}+O(n^{-3/2}).$$
One can perform this expansion with the Appendix D truncation $\hat v\ge v/4$. The removed event has exponentially small probability, so a polynomial union bound shows that the truncated and original sequences agree over $T=n^2$ times with probability tending to one.

Now use the full window in statistic (13). For every allowed $\beta$, its normalization reduces to
$$W_n=T^{-1/2}\sum_{t=1}^{T} Z_{n,t},\qquad T=n^2.$$
This horizon is permitted by Assumption 1 with $\rho=2$. Independence across times and the preceding expansion give
$$\mathbb E W_n\sim0.606191732\sqrt n,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(W_n)\longrightarrow1.$$
Hence $W_n$ exceeds any fixed finite Brownian threshold with probability tending to one. Since the monitoring statistic includes this full-window candidate, the claimed false-alarm guarantee cannot hold at the stated polynomial horizons. In Appendix D, the omitted off-diagonal products of studentization errors are nonzero because the individual errors have nonzero means. Stabilizing the denominator below its typical value does not remove this accumulated bias.
checks.repair:
The repair must control the score's mean over the whole monitoring horizon. For the boundary mechanism above,
$$\sqrt T\,\mathbb E Z_n=0.606191732\ldots\sqrt{T/n}+O(\sqrt T\,n^{-3/2}).$$
Thus $T=o(n)$ removes this accumulated-mean obstruction. It does not by itself prove the original maximum-over-windows guarantee, which also requires uniform control of the centered process.

With known population variance $v$, the replacement
$$Z_n^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt n(\hat p-3\hat q)}{\sqrt v}$$
has $\mathbb E Z_n^{\circ}=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z_n^{\circ})=1$ exactly at this boundary: its numerator has mean zero and variance $v$. This removes the exhibited studentization bias but changes the procedure. A denominator floor below the typical standard-error scale leaves that bias in place.
checks.scope: Theorem 1(i) fails under its allowed polynomial horizons, already when the same mechanism is used at every time with independent sampling. The construction concerns false-alarm control; it does not establish the separate detection-power or delay statements.
checks.title: Studentization bias invalidates the polynomial-horizon false-alarm guarantee
checks.whyItMatters: The failed statement is the central guarantee that the monitoring procedure controls false alarms over time.
checks.claimContext: Theorem 1(i) states that the monitoring procedure has asymptotic false-alarm probability at most $\alpha\in(0,1)$ whenever every true privacy gap is nonpositive. Assumption 1 permits any fixed polynomial horizon, $T(n)/n^\rho\to c_T\in(0,\infty)$ with $\rho\geq0$, in the per-time sample size $n$. The counterexample uses the same mechanism at every time, independent samples at every time, and $T=n^2$.
checks.checkedLocation: Assumption 1; Theorem 1(i); equations (7), (8), (13); Appendix D, C1-C2 calculation

checks.claim: In this case, by construction, also $\hat{p}_{t}=0$ and we may interpret the ratio $\hat{p}_{t}/\hat{\sigma}_{t}=0/0=0$ .
checks.explanation: Each empirical binomial variance vanishes at both endpoint counts, $0$ and $n$. The two samples can reach different endpoints. Then the denominator is zero while the numerator is nonzero, so the asserted $0/0$ convention does not define all possible scores.
checks.demonstration:
Write $N_X=n_t^X$, $N_Y=n_t^Y$ and $a=e^\varepsilon\geq1$. The definitions give
$$\hat p_t=\frac{N_X-aN_Y}{n},\qquad
\hat\sigma_t^2=\frac{N_X}{n^2}\left(1-\frac{N_X}{n}\right)+\frac{a^2N_Y}{n^2}\left(1-\frac{N_Y}{n}\right).$$
Both summands are nonnegative. Hence $\hat\sigma_t=0$ exactly when $N_X,N_Y\in\{0,n\}$. In particular,
$$(N_X,N_Y)=(n,0)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\hat\sigma_t=0,\qquad\hat p_t=1.$$
This event can occur under the null hypothesis. Take a binary mechanism that ignores its input and returns one with probability $1/2$. It satisfies $\varepsilon$-DP for every $\varepsilon\geq0$, and its true gap is $(1-a)/2\leq0$. With the paper's independent sampling, the displayed count pair has probability $2^{-n}2^{-n}=4^{-n}>0$. Thus the failure is present for every finite sample size, including when privacy holds.
checks.repair:
Use the positive floor already proposed in equation (16) for every score:
$$\tilde\sigma_t(c_n)=\max(\hat\sigma_t,c_n),\qquad c_n>0,\qquad Z_t=\frac{\hat p_t}{\tilde\sigma_t(c_n)}.$$
Since $-a\leq\hat p_t\leq1$, this gives $|Z_t|\leq a/c_n<\infty$ for all possible counts. On the witness it gives $Z_t=1/c_n$, rather than treating a nonzero numerator as zero. This proves that the rule is defined; calibration of the resulting monitoring statistic is a separate question.
checks.scope: The false statement is the zero-variance implication in Section 3.1, and the resulting undefined-score event affects the unfloored score used by Algorithm 1, line 3, and statistic (13). The optional positive floor in equation (16) supplies a complete definition for the stabilized variant considered in Corollary 1. That replacement does not remove the accumulated studentization bias identified in the separate Theorem 1(i) counterexample.
checks.title: Zero estimated variance does not force a zero privacy score
checks.claimContext: Section 3.1 forms a privacy score from two independent samples of size $n\geq1$. Equations (7) and (8) define the empirical gap $\hat p_t$ and its estimated standard deviation $\hat\sigma_t$. The variance-stabilization paragraph claims that $\hat\sigma_t=0$ forces $\hat p_t=0$, so the ratio can be set to zero. Algorithm 1, line 3, and statistic (13) use this unfloored score. Equation (16) separately proposes a positive denominator floor; Corollary 1 concerns the variant obtained by making that replacement.
checks.whyItMatters: The unstabilized score can have a nonzero numerator and a zero denominator on samples permitted by the model.
checks.checkedLocation: arXiv v1 · Section 3.1, equations (7), (8), and the variance-stabilization paragraph before equation (16).

checks.explanation: Token commitment changes the set $M_t$ of summands. Removing a positive contribution can make the factorised gap negative while every logit remains constant. Equation (7) differentiates the logits but omits the resulting jump in the sum, so its integration cannot bound all endpoint crossings by logit motion alone.
checks.demonstration:
Consider an interval $[1/4,3/4]$ after decoding has already begun, with two positions still masked. At the first position, assign total probability $0.72$ to refusal tokens and $0.18$ to compliance tokens; at the second, assign masses $0.30$ and $0.60$. Put the remaining probability $0.10$ at other tokens. Within each group, distribute mass positively across its tokens. This realizes the paper's refusal and compliance sets with finite, constant logits and independent per-position predictions.

Before time $1/2$, the two contributions are
$$\phi_1=\log 4,\qquad \phi_2=-\log 2,\qquad \Delta E_{\mathrm F}=\log 2.$$
At time $1/2$, commit the first position and remove it from $M_t$. Leave all logits constant. The remaining gap is $\Delta E_{\mathrm F}=-\log 2$. Thus the gap crosses from at least $+\delta$ to at most $-\delta$ for $\delta=0.6$.

Every logit velocity is zero, so the kinetic integral is zero with $\gamma_t=t$ and $\dot\gamma_t=1$. For a log ratio of two disjoint token-group masses $q_{\mathrm{ref}},q_{\mathrm{comp}}$, the Fisher norm is
$$\|\nabla_p\phi\|_F^2=\frac1{q_{\mathrm{ref}}}+\frac1{q_{\mathrm{comp}}}.$$
Consequently $G_{\max}^2=125/18$, $|M|_{\max}=2$ and $t_2-t_1=1/2$. Equation (9) requires kinetic energy at least $0.20736$, contradicting the zero integral. The whole change comes from the removed contribution, a jump of $-\log4$. Starting the example after the initial state also avoids relying on any claim about exchangeability at the fully masked state.
checks.repair:
Require a fixed mask and an absolutely continuous logit path on the interval. Then the chain rule and Cauchy–Schwarz used in Appendix A.2 give
$$|\dot{\Delta E}_{\mathrm F}(t)|^2\leq |M|G_{\max}^2\sum_{i\in M}\dot z_i^\top F(z_i)\dot z_i.$$
Integrating, using $\int|\dot{\Delta E}_{\mathrm F}|\,dt\geq2\delta$ and $0<\dot\gamma_t\leq1$, proves the original lower bound for that restricted setting.

For a changing mask and piecewise absolutely continuous logits, retain the jumps explicitly. Let $J=\sum_\tau[\Delta E_{\mathrm F}(\tau^+)-\Delta E_{\mathrm F}(\tau^-)]$ be their signed total, including changes caused by committing tokens. If $K$ denotes the kinetic integral and $T=t_2-t_1$, the same argument gives
$$K\geq\frac{\left|\Delta E_{\mathrm F}(t_2)-\Delta E_{\mathrm F}(t_1)-J\right|^2}{T\,|M|_{\max}G_{\max}^2}
\geq\frac{(2\delta-|J|)_+^2}{T\,|M|_{\max}G_{\max}^2},$$
where $(u)_+=\max(u,0)$. In the example, the corrected lower bound is zero. A positive kinetic guarantee across token commitments therefore requires a bound on their total jump contribution.
checks.scope: Theorem 1 fails for the moving-mask gap in Definition 2. The original lower bound holds for a fixed mask and an absolutely continuous logit path; the corrected bound allows piecewise absolutely continuous paths and subtracts their signed jump total $J$. A positive guarantee across token commitments requires control of $J$. The construction is a mathematical counterexample, not evidence of a successful model jailbreak.

checks.demonstration:
Let $z_0=(5,0,-5)$, $R=\sqrt{50}$, $u=(0,1,0)$ and $v=(1,0,1)/\sqrt2$. Both $u$ and $v$ are unit tangent directions to the sphere at $z_0$. Define
$$z_A=\cos(\varepsilon)z_0+R\sin(\varepsilon)u,\qquad z_B=\cos(6\varepsilon/5)z_0+R\sin(6\varepsilon/5)v.$$
Both norms equal $R$ exactly, and $z_B$ has smaller cosine with $z_0$. For $F_0=\operatorname{diag}(p_0)-p_0p_0^\top$, the identity $F_0\mathbf1=0$ and $v=(\mathbf1-u)/\sqrt2$ give $v^\top F_0v=u^\top F_0u/2>0$. The source's valid second-order KL expansion therefore gives
$$\frac{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_B\|p_0)}{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_A\|p_0)}\longrightarrow\frac{(6/5)^2}{2}=\frac{18}{25}<1.$$
For sufficiently small positive $\varepsilon$, the larger angular displacement has smaller KL divergence. A path on the same sphere can join these two nearby points.
checks.repair:
Replace monotonicity by explicit metric bounds. Fix the additive logit gauge and suppose a subspace containing $\delta=z-z_0$ has Fisher eigenvalues between $0<m\le M$ along the whole segment $z_0+s\delta$, $0\le s\le1$. The exact identity
$$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_z\|p_{z_0})=\int_0^1 s\,\delta^\top F(z_0+s\delta)\delta\,ds$$
gives $m\|\delta\|^2/2\le D_{\mathrm{KL}}\le M\|\delta\|^2/2$. At equal norms $R$, these become bounds by $mR^2(1-\cos)$ and $MR^2(1-\cos)$. Different constants do not establish an ordering between arbitrary directions; monotonicity needs further direction or isotropy assumptions. To approximate kinetic energy, use controlled increments between adjacent times divided by the time step, with a discretization bound, rather than cumulative displacement from time zero.
